statement: In bodies examined after death, the measured concentration of a drug in blood can differ from the concentration at the moment of death, and from one blood vessel to another in the same body, by amounts that vary between drugs and between bodies and that cannot be predicted for a given death. In four suspected overdose deaths chosen by forensic medicine authors in Dundee and Edmonton to illustrate the problem (tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and the sleeping medicine flurazepam; autopsy about 7 to 48 hours after death; office and period not stated), blood drawn separately from up to 11 vessels of the same body differed 3.5- to 6.6-fold for each drug (editors' calculation from the printed ranges), usually highest in central vessels near the lungs and liver and lowest in the subclavian or femoral veins, though in one case the lowest value was in the pulmonary artery; in the only person with a blood sample from life, taken in hospital about 1 to 2 hours before death, every post-mortem sample, femoral blood included, held 1.8 to 7.9 times as much imipramine (editors' calculation). The authors attribute the differences to drug diffusing out of organs after death, but no body was sampled more than once and unabsorbed drug was still in the gut in three of the four, so part of the differences may have arisen before death (Pounder & Jones, 1990). A compilation of 10,993 results from 5,375 post-mortem cases for 50 compounds (published reports found by keyword searching, plus a Finnish national laboratory database for 2000 to 2018; cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids were left out) found, where the same case had both values, median ratios to femoral blood across drugs of 1.27 for other blood such as heart blood (576 results), 0.99 for muscle, 0.45 for the fluid of the eye (vitreous humour), 1.84 for brain, 2.03 for heart muscle, 5.06 for liver and 5.52 for bile, with tenfold or larger differences between drugs for most specimens (for other blood, morphine 1.26 and methamphetamine 1.50); no range or interval is given for any ratio, and cause of death and time since death could not be taken into account (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019). A review of 87 studies selected from a two-database search in April 2025 reports that in animal experiments drug levels in heart blood rose within minutes of death; that in human bodies sampled more than once, femoral blood, the sample thought least open to change (Ferner, 2008), rose significantly after death for about a dozen drugs, among them fentanyl and methadone, and fell for others, among them 6-MAM (the marker of heroin) and THC; and that the first sample in these human studies was taken on average about 17 hours after death (range 1 to 292 hours), so earlier change was not seen. It gives no sizes, does not appraise the studies, judges that a heart-to-femoral blood ratio shows that change after death occurred but not how much, and concludes that the size of the change cannot yet be tied to drug properties or to features of the case (Borra et al., 2026). A 2003 practitioners' review lists single approximate heart-to-peripheral blood ratios for about 100 drugs without case numbers or sources (for example morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3), higher than the compilation's paired medians for several of the same drugs (Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ketola & Kriikku, 2019), and a clinical pharmacologist's review adds that post-mortem whole blood is compared with plasma or serum values from living patients, and that the ratio between the two differs by drug even in life (Ferner, 2008). Change can run both ways: a level after death can be higher than in life, which can make a drug look more involved in a death than it was, or lower, for drugs that break down or are lost after death. The evidence consists of selected case series, an unappraised compilation dominated by published poisoning cases, and narrative reviews, mostly about medicines; how often, and by how much, a level changes in an ordinary death is not known. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Can the amount of a drug in the blood change after death? Yes. In bodies examined after death, the amount of a drug was often different depending on which blood vessel the blood came from: in four overdose deaths, from about 3 to 7 times, usually higher near the heart, lungs and liver than in the thigh. In one person tested in hospital before death, every sample taken after death was about 2 to 8 times higher. In about 5,000 cases collected from many studies, blood from other sites, such as the heart, held on average about a quarter more drug than thigh blood, with big differences between drugs. Levels in thigh blood also rose or fell in the hours after death for some drugs, and the first sample was often taken many hours after death. So a level after death can make a drug look more, or less, involved than it was. Most of this comes from small or selected studies, mostly of medicines.
population: Bodies examined after death: four selected suspected overdose deaths at medico-legal autopsy (Pounder & Jones, 1990); 5,375 post-mortem cases from published reports and a Finnish laboratory database, 2000 to 2018 (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019); animal experiments and human bodies sampled more than once, as reviewed (Borra et al., 2026); narrative reviews (Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ferner, 2008)
exposure: Drug concentration measured after death in blood from different vessels and in other specimens, and at different times after death
comparator: Femoral (thigh vein) blood from the same body; a blood sample taken in life (one case); earlier samples from the same body
outcome: Size and direction of differences in measured drug concentration between sampling sites and over time after death
magnitude: Within one body (four selected overdoses): highest to lowest blood value 3.5- to 6.6-fold per drug (editors' calculation; doxepin 3.5, amobarbital 6.0, secobarbital 6.5, pentobarbital 6.2, clomipramine 5.4, flurazepam 6.6, imipramine 4.4; lidocaine given in hospital 1.6). One case with a sample from life: post-mortem imipramine 4.1–18.1 mg/L against 2.3 mg/L in hospital, 1.8- to 7.9-fold. Paired median ratios to femoral blood across drugs (number of results): other blood 1.27 (576), muscle 0.99 (385), vitreous humour 0.45 (356), brain 1.84 (565), heart 2.03 (185), kidney 2.86 (401), lung 3.69 (187), spleen 4.25 (71), liver 5.06 (1,697), bile 5.52 (537); between drugs, liver 0.95–54.29, vitreous 0.03–1.59, other blood 0.90–14.61; other blood for morphine 1.26 (53), methamphetamine 1.50 (9). Human repeated sampling: first sample on average 17 h after death (range 1–292 h); rises in femoral blood for about 12 drugs, falls for 5 (no sizes). Single heart-to-peripheral ratios without case numbers (narrative review): morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5–2.3. No intervals anywhere.

risk_of_bias.note: The site differences come from four overdose deaths chosen to illustrate the problem, with no denominator and no serial sampling (card sc_pounder_1990, JBI high); the ratios come from a compilation dominated by published poisoning cases, without appraisal, weighting or spread (card sc_ketola_2019, AMSTAR 2 by analogy, critically low); the changes over time are relayed without sizes from a review that does not appraise its studies (card sc_borra_2026). Selection of striking cases could make the differences look larger than in ordinary deaths.

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: every source points the same way (levels differ by site and change after death); the size varies by drug, which the claim states rather than hides.

indirectness.note: The question concerns deaths involving any drug, including drugs used outside medicine; the compilation excludes cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids, the case series concerns large overdoses of medicines with drug still in the gut, and part of the evidence on timing is from animals.

imprecision.note: Four cases; no ranges, percentiles or intervals for any compiled ratio; many drug–specimen ratios rest on one to three results.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for case series and compilations of case literature.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, which reaches the floor: very low. Strict reading: that drug levels can differ between sampling sites and change after death is shown consistently by independent designs (a case series with a sample from life, a large compilation of paired values, repeated-sampling studies as reviewed) and on its own would be rated low; the sizes, and how often a change matters in an ordinary death, are very low. Status replicated: Pounder & Jones and the primary studies compiled by Ketola & Kriikku and reviewed by Borra et al. are independent and agree in direction. Counted once: Pounder & Jones is one of the compilation's doxepin sources; Ferner (2008) takes its heart-to-femoral ratios from Leikin & Watson (2003), so the narrative reviews' ratios are one source, used only as second-hand examples.

verification.flag_note: Question 5 is split in two (this claim: whether levels change after death and with the sampling site; cl_gen_deaths_level_cause: whether a level can show cause), because the evidence differs in kind. Rests on a case series, an unappraised compilation of case literature (AMSTAR 2 critically low) and narrative reviews; no study measured change after death in consecutive ordinary deaths. The Leikin & Watson ratios are single values without sources.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether cannabis use causes sudden deaths from heart or blood-vessel problems, and in the one large autopsy registry read here no death was certified as a poisoning by THC, the main active substance of cannabis. A 2019 narrative review by three forensic medicine authors in Victoria, Australia (English-language reports found in two databases, with no stated selection rules or appraisal) counted six publications describing 13 deaths, all of men aged 17 to 52, that the case authors, and in one case a coroner, linked to recent cannabis use: 8 of the 13 had significant coronary artery disease or other pathology, THC was measured in blood in 8 (1.9 to 22 ng/mL), the other 5 rested on urine tests or the person's history (in one of them no THC was found in blood, yet the coroner found cannabis a secondary cause), alcohol was found in 2, two died days after reaching hospital and one had no autopsy (Drummer et al., 2019). The reviewers write that the larger studies and systematic reviews leave the link between cannabis use and death from heart disease unclear and the risk probably rare, that no minimum blood THC level can show cause because of delays between death and sampling (most laboratories detect 1 to 2 ng/mL, and lower values may reflect use days earlier), and that a blood THC test, not urine or history alone, is needed to link a death to recent use; yet they recommend that, with very recent use, a positive blood THC and a possible heart or brain-vessel cause, cannabis be considered at least a contributory cause of a sudden death, that THC be recorded in death statistics, and they call the 13 deaths 'very likely to be an under-estimate of the true incidence', without data on how many deaths are missed (Drummer et al., 2019). The review also notes, without details or numbers, that some deaths have been attributed to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (severe repeated vomiting; four references, not read here; Drummer et al., 2019). They relay, second-hand, studies pointing both ways: a heart-attack risk 4.8 times the baseline (95% CI 2.9 to 9.5) in the hour after smoking cannabis in a case-crossover study of 3,882 people, and a higher death rate after a heart attack with weekly use (hazard ratio 4.2, 1.2 to 14, in 1,913 people), against no association with death from heart disease in 5,113 young US adults followed for 25 years, and two systematic reviews that disagree; the review's statement that eleven of its twelve tabulated studies showed raised risk is not borne out by its own table (Drummer et al., 2019). In Finland, among 57,903 medico-legal autopsies with full drug testing in 2000 to 2010, THC was found in femoral blood in 347 deaths (median 0.002 mg/L, that is 2 ng/mL), and forensic pathologists certified none of them as a fatal poisoning with THC as the main finding (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014). THC levels after death are hard to read: THC in femoral blood fell after death in bodies sampled more than once (Borra et al., 2026, relayed without sizes), and whole blood, the usual post-mortem sample, has to be multiplied by about 1.6 to compare with the plasma values used for living people (Leikin & Watson, 2003, second-hand). The case reports have no comparison group and cannot show how often THC is present in sudden deaths that cannabis did not cause, so counting cannabis as a cause on the reviewers' criteria would rest on THC being present plus the circumstances. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Can cannabis cause death? In the studies read here, no death was put down to cannabis poisoning alone: in Finland, none of 347 people who died with THC in their blood (2000 to 2010) was counted as a THC poisoning. Published reports describe 13 men who died suddenly soon after using cannabis, mostly from heart problems; 8 already had heart disease or other illness, alcohol was found in 2, and 5 had no blood test showing recent use. Whether cannabis caused these deaths cannot be shown. Studies of heart attacks point both ways: one found more heart attacks in the hour after smoking cannabis, while a 25-year study found no link with heart deaths. Some deaths have also been put down to a severe vomiting illness linked to cannabis, but no numbers are given. The forensic doctors who wrote the review want cannabis counted as a contributing cause in such deaths and think deaths are missed, but give no numbers. See the contested question.
population: Published case reports of deaths linked to recent cannabis use (13 men aged 17–52 in 6 publications, compiled in 2019); 57,903 Finnish medico-legal autopsies with full drug testing, 2000–2010 (347 with THC in femoral blood); epidemiological studies of heart attack, stroke and death, second-hand
exposure: Recent cannabis use, shown by THC in blood, urine cannabinoids or history
comparator: None in the case reports; deaths not certified as THC poisoning in the registry; control periods or people not using cannabis in the epidemiological studies relayed
outcome: Sudden death from heart or brain-vessel causes put down to cannabis; certification of a death as THC poisoning
magnitude: Not estimable as a risk. Case reports (Drummer et al., 2019): 13 deaths, men aged 17–52 (median 37); coronary disease or other pathology 8/13; blood THC measured in 8 (1.9–22 ng/mL), urine or history only in 5 (one blood-negative); alcohol in 2 (0.04% and 0.119%). Relayed: acute myocardial infarction 4.8 (95% CI 2.9–9.5) within 1 h of smoking, 1.7 (0.6–5.1) within 2 h (case-crossover, n = 3,882); mortality after MI, HR 4.2 (1.2–14) weekly use, 2.5 (0.9–7.3) less than weekly (n = 1,913); CARDIA (n = 5,113, 25 years): no association with cardiovascular mortality. Finland 2000–2010: THC in femoral blood in 347 deaths, median 0.002 mg/L, 97.5th percentile 0.024 mg/L, 0% certified as THC poisoning.

No search dates, numbers screened or appraisal method are given.

risk_of_bias.note: The deaths are published case reports, chosen by their authors for a suspected link and not appraised by the review (card sc_drummer_2019, editors' checklist high); certification in the registry rests on pathologists' judgment without stated criteria (card sc_launiainen_2014).

inconsistency.note: The epidemiological studies relayed point in different directions (raised heart-attack risk in the hour after use and higher death rates after a heart attack, against no association with cardiovascular death in a 25-year cohort and a systematic review finding no compelling link with mortality).

indirectness.note: The epidemiology is known only through a narrative review and mostly concerns heart attack and stroke, not death; the case reports span decades and several countries; five of the 13 deaths lack the blood test the reviewers themselves require.

imprecision.note: Thirteen deaths with no denominator or comparison group; no estimate of a death risk exists in the sources read.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; case reports are published because a link was suspected, which the risk-of-bias rating covers.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Status contested: the forensic reviewers' recommendation to count cannabis as a contributory cause and their view that such deaths are undercounted meet their own statement that the link is unclear, a 25-year cohort with no association and a registry in which none of 347 deaths with THC was certified as THC poisoning; the six-part debate box applies. The two systematic reviews and the cohort studies are known only through Drummer et al. and are not counted as replication. The claim gives no advice and makes no statement about amounts.

debate.question: Can using cannabis cause a sudden death, for example by setting off a heart attack or a dangerous heart rhythm, and should such deaths be counted as cannabis deaths?
debate.evidence_yes: Case reports describe 13 men aged 17 to 52 whose deaths their authors linked to recent cannabis use, 8 of them with THC measured in blood (1.9 to 22 ng/mL) and five described as having little obvious heart disease; in one case a coroner found cannabis a secondary cause of death (Drummer et al., 2019). The same review describes 35 people in 31 case reports who reached hospital with heart attacks (18 confirmed by blood tests), rhythm problems or strokes during or soon after cannabis use, 24 of them without evidence of coronary artery disease (Drummer et al., 2019). As relayed, a case-crossover study of 3,882 people with a heart attack found a risk 4.8 times the baseline (95% CI 2.9 to 9.5) in the hour after smoking cannabis; among 1,913 people after a heart attack the death rate was higher with weekly use (hazard ratio 4.2, 1.2 to 14); in national hospital data ischaemic stroke was more common (adjusted risk ratio 1.17, 1.15 to 1.20); among 2,097 people with a heart attack before age 51, cardiovascular death was more common (adjusted hazard ratio 2.22, printed as a 90% CI of 1.27 to 3.70); and a systematic review of 81 case reports and 29 observational studies found an association with cardiovascular disease, stronger for ischaemic stroke (Drummer et al., 2019). The review also notes, without numbers, deaths attributed to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (Drummer et al., 2019). The forensic reviewers hold that a small number of susceptible people with other illnesses could be harmed, and that when use was very recent, blood THC is positive and the death could be cardiac or cerebrovascular, cannabis should be recorded as at least a contributory cause so that its harm is not underestimated (Drummer et al., 2019).
debate.evidence_no: In the Finnish autopsy registry, none of 347 deaths with THC in femoral blood in 2000 to 2010 was certified as a THC poisoning (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014). Of the 13 published deaths, 8 had significant coronary disease or other pathology, alcohol was found in 2 (blood alcohol 0.04% and 0.119%), 5 lacked the blood THC result that the reviewers themselves require to link a death to recent use, one had no THC in blood, two died days after reaching hospital and one had no autopsy (Drummer et al., 2019). The reviewers state that the link with death from heart disease is not clear, that the events described may have other causes such as undiagnosed rhythm disorders or tobacco smoking, and that the risk is probably rare (Drummer et al., 2019). As relayed, the CARDIA cohort of 5,113 young US adults followed for 25 years found no association of cannabis use with cardiovascular death; a cohort of 3,886 people followed for 18 years found 29% higher mortality with cannabis use that was not statistically significant; and a systematic review found no compelling evidence linking cannabis use with death, including from heart attack (Drummer et al., 2019). The review's count of eleven of twelve studies showing raised risk is not borne out by its own table, in which at most 8 rows report a raised estimate, some not significant (first reader's reading of Drummer et al., 2019).
debate.neither_can_show: Case reports are published because someone suspected a link; deaths with THC present that were judged unrelated go unpublished, so the reports cannot show how often a link is real or how often THC is found in sudden deaths in general, and they have no comparison group. THC in blood after death does not show when cannabis was used or how much: no minimum level marks recent use or cause, laboratories detect down to 1 to 2 ng/mL, low values may reflect use days earlier, THC levels change after death, and whole blood differs from the serum used for living values (Drummer et al., 2019; Borra et al., 2026; Leikin & Watson, 2003). Certification in the registry rests on pathologists' judgment without stated criteria, so a death set off by cannabis could be put down to heart disease, and a death in which cannabis was only present could be put down to cannabis. The epidemiological studies rely mostly on self-reported use or hospital coding, are known here only second-hand, and measure heart attacks and strokes more often than deaths.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In the sources read, no death was put down to cannabis poisoning on its own. The deaths linked to cannabis are a small number of sudden heart or brain-vessel deaths soon after use, mostly in men who already had heart disease, sometimes with alcohol, and several without a blood test showing recent use. Whether cannabis set off any of them cannot be shown from case reports, and the population studies relayed by the review point both ways, mostly for heart attacks rather than deaths. The forensic reviewers' call to count cannabis as a contributory cause, and their view that such deaths are undercounted, are positions without data on how many deaths are missed or on how often THC is present in deaths it did not cause; applied in certification, they would raise counts of cannabis deaths on the strength of THC being present plus the circumstances.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A population-based study of sudden cardiac deaths with complete toxicology (blood THC with the time from death to sampling recorded), compared with suitable controls such as deaths from external causes or living people from the same population, with coronary disease, tobacco and alcohol measured, to estimate whether recent cannabis use raises the risk of sudden cardiac death and how often THC is present in such deaths without having contributed; and agreement studies of certification rules for drug contribution, tested on pathologists who do not know the toxicology results.

statement: Deaths recorded as heroin 'overdoses' often involve other drugs, delays and other mechanisms, so the label does not show that heroin alone caused the death, but which substance or mechanism was decisive in a given death cannot be read from the toxicology. In a 1996 narrative review of medical examiners' and coroners' series and official statistics, mostly from 1967 to 1996 in the USA, Australia and Europe, chosen by the authors without a stated search and leaning on their own New South Wales series of 152 heroin-related deaths in 1992, morphine (the substance heroin becomes in the body) was the only drug detected at autopsy in 23% to 48% of deaths attributed to heroin overdose across six studies; alcohol was detected in 29% to 75% across 13 studies, with mean blood alcohol of 0.09 to 0.16 g/100 mL where reported, and benzodiazepines in 12% to 55% across four; which drugs each laboratory looked for, and how each source defined a heroin death, is not given (Darke & Zador, 1996, second-hand). Blood morphine was lower in deaths with alcohol in the five studies that compared them, with weak correlations where reported (r = −0.14 in 505 deaths; r = −0.28 in the authors' series); a third of the authors' series had morphine below the laboratories' toxic level for people without opioid tolerance (0.16 mg/L); and a 1977 Michigan series found 74% with morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died of other causes (Darke & Zador, 1996). Many deaths were not instant: 14% of the authors' series were classed as instant and 22% took more than 3 hours, other series found intervals of more than 2 or 3 hours in 44% and 52%, and other people were present at more than half of the deaths in four studies (58% to 79% where a figure was given; Darke & Zador, 1996). The reviewers write that 'overdose' 'may correctly apply to only a minority of heroin-related deaths' and propose 'multiple drug toxicity' for many of them; but finding other drugs does not show that they caused the death, the comparison with survivors rests on three studies cited without figures, tolerance was measured in no study, and low morphine can also reflect a death hours after the last injection, when morphine had already fallen, or change after death (Darke & Zador, 1996). In England and Wales in 2000, of 1,037 accidental drug-related deaths that coroners reported to a national register (the National Programme of Substance Abuse Deaths; reporting voluntary, coverage not stated), the register's researchers classed 802 (77%) as direct overdoses and 235 (23%) as other mechanisms: choking on stomach contents and other acute events (74), drug toxicity on top of a medical condition (112), injuries (31) and infections (18). Heroin or morphine was named as implicated in 424 of the direct overdoses and found after death in 488, and was implicated in 42 of the 74 acute events, 33 of the 72 deaths with a drug-related medical condition and 11 of the 18 infections; alcohol was found after death in 316 (39.4%) of the direct overdoses; methadone was implicated in 13% of direct overdoses but was the only drug implicated in 4%. These figures are the researchers' reading of coroners' returns that recorded only drugs found, not a check of official statistics, which were not compared (Webb et al., 2003). In the other direction, heroin can be missed: 6-MAM, the marker that shows heroin rather than another source of morphine, fell in femoral blood after death in bodies sampled more than once (Borra et al., 2026), and a review table reports, second-hand, that testing the fluid around the brain and spinal cord for 6-MAM detected 46% more heroin-related deaths than testing blood (Leikin & Watson, 2003). The evidence is old (before fentanyl), largely second-hand, and from series chosen by the authors or from a register. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Are deaths called heroin 'overdoses' always caused by heroin alone? Often not, but tests after death cannot show which drug mattered most. In older studies from the USA, Australia and Europe (1967 to 1996), heroin (found as morphine) was the only drug found in about 23 to 48 in 100 deaths called heroin overdoses. Alcohol was found in about 29 to 75 in 100, and sleeping or calming pills (benzodiazepines) in 12 to 55 in 100. Many people did not die at once: in one series, about 1 in 5 took more than 3 hours to die, and other people were often there. In England and Wales in 2000, about 1 in 4 accidental deaths that coroners linked to drugs were not simple overdoses: they involved choking on vomit, an illness, an injury or an infection, often with heroin involved. Heroin can also be missed, because its marker breaks down after death. These studies are old, from before fentanyl.
population: Deaths attributed to heroin overdose by medical examiners, coroners or researchers in series from the USA, Australia and Europe, mostly 1967–1996 (second-hand, Darke & Zador, 1996); 1,037 accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners in England and Wales to a national register in 2000 (Webb et al., 2003)
exposure: Heroin use, shown by morphine (and where tested 6-MAM) found after death; other drugs found or named as implicated
comparator: Deaths with morphine as the only drug; people who used heroin and died of other causes (one 1977 series, second-hand); direct overdoses against other mechanisms in the register
outcome: What else was found in deaths attributed to heroin overdose, the timing and circumstances of death, and the mechanism of death
magnitude: Morphine the only drug detected: 23%–48% of deaths attributed to heroin overdose (six studies); alcohol detected 29%–75% (13 studies), mean blood alcohol 0.09–0.16 g/100 mL; benzodiazepines 12%–55% (four studies). Morphine lower with alcohol: r = −0.14 (505 deaths), −0.28. A third below 0.16 mg/L (one series); 74% no higher than people who used heroin and died of other causes (one 1977 series). Instant deaths 14% and over 3 h 22% (one series); over 2 h 44%, over 3 h 52% (two series); others present 58%–79%. All second-hand, no intervals. England and Wales 2000 (1,037 accidental deaths): direct overdose 802 (77%); other mechanisms 235 (23%); heroin/morphine implicated in 424 and found in 488 direct overdoses; implicated in 42/74 acute events, 33/72 drug-related medical conditions, 11/18 infections; alcohol found in 316 (39.4%) direct overdoses; methadone implicated in 13% of direct overdoses, the only drug implicated in 4%. 6-MAM in cerebrospinal fluid: 46% more heroin-related deaths detected than in blood (second-hand).

risk_of_bias.note: The review chooses its studies without a stated search, leans on the authors' own series and does not appraise any study; laboratory panels and case definitions are unknown (card sc_darke_1996, editors' checklist high). The register is voluntary with unstated coverage, and its categories are the researchers' unvalidated reading of coroners' returns (phi 0.77 overall; card sc_webb_2003, JBI high).

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: the shares vary widely between studies, as expected from different panels, places and decades, but all point the same way (other drugs are often present in deaths attributed to heroin).

indirectness.note: Most figures are second-hand and from 1967 to 2000, before fentanyl and other synthetic opioids changed what is found in opioid deaths; the register covers England and Wales in one year.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded: the claim gives ranges across studies, not a single estimate.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); down for risk of bias and indirectness: very low. Status replicated: the series that Darke & Zador relay (from several countries and decades) and the England and Wales register are independent and agree that deaths attributed to heroin often involve other drugs or other mechanisms. The claim describes what was found together with heroin; it does not say that alcohol or benzodiazepines caused any death, and it gives no advice on amounts or combinations.
